I'll work through the draft systematically, applying each test to passages where compression might have damaged structure.

---

**Ch 011 draft — checking the escape sequence**

The draft cuts the source's sheet-as-weapon gambit entirely. In the source, the narrator grabs a bedsheet, shrieks about a badger, lures the servants to the door, throws the sheet over the old woman, shoves everyone into a tangle, and escapes into the hall — then ducks through the *front-hall door* into the lord's adjoining room. The draft cuts all of that and replaces it with a quiet slip through the side door she noticed was there.

That's fine on its own — but look at the dialogue exchange that survives:

> "Only a moment ago."

In the source the old woman completes: *"Only a moment ago, and she—well, she threw a blanket over my husband and me."* The detail about the blanket is the old woman's embarrassed admission that explains why the search was delayed and why the lord finds it amusing. The draft cuts it.

Does cutting that admission break anything structurally? The lord's response is:

> "I see. There is no further cause for concern. She is found and that is all that needs be done on your part."

His "I see" and the merriment in his tone still parse — he knows she's under the bed (via the mark), so the amusement is slightly undermotivated but not unreadable. The reader can follow without the blanket detail. Not a valid finding.

---

**Ch 011 draft — the side-door approach**

In the source the narrator explicitly notices the side door from her *own* room, rules it out initially ("The side one obviously led to another room which wasn't what I wanted"), tries the front door, finds it locked, screams, executes the sheet plan, escapes into the *hall*, then as a last resort ducks into the *hall door* that happens to connect to the lord's room — she had forgotten the side door connected there. The dramatic irony is that she ends up exactly where the side door would have taken her.

The draft replaces this with: she tries the window, tries the front door, then — with no mention of the screaming/sheet plan — simply opens the side door and walks through into the lord's room.

But crucially, the draft never establishes that she tried and failed at screaming or any other escape. The passage reads:

> "I pressed my ear to the main door... I rapped the wood, called once, got nothing useful back but the cold. Panic nipped at me. All right—if the main way out was locked, then through the side door to anywhere but here. The side door swung inward on a quiet hinge."

The old woman then appears in the lord's room saying "the girl has once again escaped." But in the draft, the narrator never *did* escape — she just walked quietly through a side door. The old woman's line "the girl has once again escaped" now refers to something that did not happen in the draft. The household is in alarm-mode ("feet gathered, keys, orders, the busy clatter of a household who had lost track of its troublesome charge") with no cause established in the draft.

**Gate test**: A reader of the draft alone sees the narrator quietly slip through a side door, then hears the household in a state of emergency searching for an escaped girl. The old woman reports she "has once again escaped." The reader has no idea what triggered the alarm — no screaming, no sheet assault, no escape into the hall. The household's agitated state and the old woman's report are genuinely unmotivated in the draft. This is a broken logical pivot: the cause (the sheet-escape that triggered the hunt) was cut, leaving its effect (the panicked household search) floating.

**Finding 1 — valid.**

---

**Ch 011 draft — "She is found"**

> "I see. There is no further cause for concern. She is found and that is all that needs be done on your part."

The lord says "she is found" — but in the draft the household didn't know where she was; she slipped quietly through a side door. In the source the lord knows because of the mark enchantment, and he explains this later. Does "she is found" parse? The enchantment explanation comes shortly after, so a reader can retroactively understand. Marginally okay. Not flagging as a separate finding — it flows from the same broken pivot above.

---

**Ch 011 draft — the old woman's husband**

In the source, when the old woman says she threw the blanket over "my husband and me," we learn the male servant was her husband. In the draft that line is cut, so "my husband and me" disappears. The draft simply has the old woman appear. No reference to a husband anywhere. No dangling pronoun results. Not a finding.

---

**Ch 011 draft — wings disappearing**

> "Somehow the wings were missing."

This appears when the narrator sees the lord naked. In the source, same sentence appears. In both source and draft, the wings were visible at the pond. The draft established the wings at the pond in Ch 010. So "somehow the wings were missing" is fully parseable with antecedent from earlier in the same draft chapter and from Ch 010 draft. Not a finding.

---

**Ch 011 draft — closing addition**

> "I reached out, helplessly, and my fingers twitched with the memory of the air those wings had cut."

This is added material not in the source; no structural damage possible from compression here.

---

**Ch 010 draft — checking for mid-scene jump issues in Ch 011**

Ch 011 draft opens with "my new chambers" — established in Ch 010 draft? The draft of Ch 010 ends with the lord catching her; it doesn't name the chambers. But the source of Ch 010 also doesn't name the chambers in the carried passage — the chambers are established in Ch 011 source's opening. So this is not a mid-scene jump caused by Ch 010 compression. Fine.
